claim: The primate basal ganglia are implicated in visual perception and attention, in addition to their traditional role in motor control.
source: Recent work has implicated the primate basal ganglia in visual perception and attention, in addition to their traditional role in motor control.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of recent work in the field, indicating it is supported by prior research.

claim: The caudate nucleus 'head' (CDh) of the striatum receives indirect anatomical connections from the superior colliculus (SC).
source: The basal ganglia, especially the caudate nucleus 'head' (CDh) of the striatum, receive indirect anatomical connections from the superior colliculus (SC), a midbrain structure that is known to play a crucial role in the control of visual attention.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge about connections between brain structures.

claim: The superior colliculus plays a crucial role in the control of visual attention.
source: The basal ganglia, especially the caudate nucleus 'head' (CDh) of the striatum, receive indirect anatomical connections from the superior colliculus (SC), a midbrain structure that is known to play a crucial role in the control of visual attention.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the SC's role in attention.

claim: SC inactivation significantly altered the attention-related modulation of CDh neurons.
source: SC inactivation significantly altered the attention-related modulation of CDh neurons and strongly impaired the classification of task-epochs based on CDh activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SC inactivation strongly impaired the classification of task-epochs based on CDh activity.
source: SC inactivation significantly altered the attention-related modulation of CDh neurons and strongly impaired the classification of task-epochs based on CDh activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the classifier analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only inactivation of SC on the same side of the brain as recorded CDh neurons, not the opposite side, altered attention-related modulation of CDh neurons.
source: Only inactivation of SC on the same side of the brain as recorded CDh neurons, not the opposite side, had these effects.
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing same-side versus opposite-side inactivation effects.

claim: Covert visual attention is the ability of primates to selectively make use of some visual inputs while ignoring the rest, without moving the eyes.
source: Covert visual attention is the ability of primates to selectively make use of some visual inputs while ignoring the rest, without moving the eyes.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Covert attention is reliably associated with changes in the speed and accuracy of behavioral reports.
source: In laboratory tests, covert attention is reliably associated with changes in the speed and accuracy of behavioral reports (Carrasco, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carrasco, 2011.

claim: The neural mechanisms for covert visual attention in primates include the modulation of neuronal activity in visual cortical areas that represent stimulus features.
source: The neural mechanisms for covert visual attention in primates include the modulation of neuronal activity in visual cortical areas that represent stimulus features (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004; Treue, 2001), as well as areas of the frontal and parietal cortex that regulate what is attended (Bisley and Goldberg, 2010; Moore and Zirnsak, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Areas of the frontal and parietal cortex regulate what is attended.
source: The neural mechanisms for covert visual attention in primates include the modulation of neuronal activity in visual cortical areas that represent stimulus features (Reynolds and Chelazzi, 2004; Treue, 2001), as well as areas of the frontal and parietal cortex that regulate what is attended (Bisley and Goldberg, 2010; Moore and Zirnsak, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bisley and Goldberg, 2010 and Moore and Zirnsak, 2017.

claim: The control of covert attention includes subcortical brain regions.
source: More recently, it has been recognized that in addition to these cortical mechanisms, the control of covert attention also includes subcortical brain regions, consistent with the idea that covert attention in primates evolved from older subcortical circuits responsible for overt orienting movements triggered by stimulus events (Krauzlis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krauzlis et al., 2018.

claim: Covert attention in primates evolved from older subcortical circuits responsible for overt orienting movements triggered by stimulus events.
source: More recently, it has been recognized that in addition to these cortical mechanisms, the control of covert attention also includes subcortical brain regions, consistent with the idea that covert attention in primates evolved from older subcortical circuits responsible for overt orienting movements triggered by stimulus events (Krauzlis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is presented as an idea consistent with recent findings, supported by citation.

claim: The superior colliculus is one of the most important subcortical structures for the control of covert visual attention in primates.
source: One of the most important subcortical structures for the control of covert visual attention in primates is the superior colliculus (SC), located in the midbrain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the SC's importance.

claim: When SC neuronal activity is perturbed by inactivation or microstimulation, performance in attention tasks is reliably altered in a spatially specific manner, even during covert tasks.
source: When SC neuronal activity is perturbed by inactivation or microstimulation, performance in attention tasks is reliably altered in a spatially specific manner, even during covert tasks (Bogadhi et al., 2019; Bollimunta et al., 2018; Cavanaugh and Wurtz, 2004; Herman et al., 2018; Lovejoy and Krauzlis, 2010; Müller et al., 2005; Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: During SC inactivation, improvements in perceptual sensitivity made possible by spatial cues are abolished.
source: During SC inactivation, improvements in perceptual sensitivity made possible by spatial cues are abolished (Lovejoy and Krauzlis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lovejoy and Krauzlis, 2017.

claim: SC inactivation prevents spatial cues from conferring a perceptual advantage, but cue-related modulation of neuronal activity in extrastriate visual cortex remains robust during inactivation.
source: Despite SC inactivation preventing spatial cues from conferring a perceptual advantage, cue-related modulation of neuronal activity in extrastriate visual cortex remains robust during inactivation (Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012.

claim: In a covert motion-change detection task, neurons in visual areas MT and MST showed the same cue-related modulation during SC inactivation as they had before.
source: Specifically, Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012 found that in a covert motion-change detection task, neurons in visual areas MT and MST showed the same cue-related modulation during SC inactivation as they had before.
evidence: This is a specific finding from Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012.

claim: SC inactivation impairs behavior by altering the use of cortical sensory signals in another brain area.
source: Because behavior in this task depends on signals arising from MT/MST, these results suggest that SC inactivation impairs behavior by altering the use of cortical sensory signals in another brain area.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings of Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012.

claim: The striatum of the basal ganglia, in particular the 'head' of the caudate nucleus (CDh), is a candidate site for where SC inactivation alters the use of cortical sensory signals.
source: One candidate site, based on the convergence of signals from visual cortex and the SC, is the striatum of the basal ganglia (Redgrave, 2010; Saint-Cyr et al., 1990), in particular, the 'head' of the caudate nucleus (CDh).
evidence: This is proposed based on anatomical convergence, supported by citations.

claim: The caudate is divided into the 'head' (CDh) at the anterior end, followed by the 'body', 'genu', and 'tail' (CDt).
source: The caudate is divided into the 'head' (CDh) at the anterior end, followed by the 'body', 'genu', and 'tail' (CDt).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge about the structure of the caudate.

claim: Different territories of the caudate have distinct functional roles consistent with the parallel functional circuit architecture of the basal ganglia.
source: In keeping with the parallel functional circuit architecture of the basal ganglia (Alexander et al., 1986), these territories appear to have distinct functional roles.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alexander et al., 1986.

claim: Inactivating CDh neurons impairs choice among visual stimuli that are flexibly associated with high or low reward but does not impair choice of stimuli with fixed reward association.
source: For example, inactivating CDh neurons impairs choice among visual stimuli that are flexibly associated with high or low reward but does not impair choice of stimuli with fixed reward association, whereas CDt inactivation impairs only choices with fixed reward association stimuli and not flexible reward (Kim and Hikosaka, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim and Hikosaka, 2013.

claim: CDt inactivation impairs only choices with fixed reward association stimuli and not flexible reward.
source: For example, inactivating CDh neurons impairs choice among visual stimuli that are flexibly associated with high or low reward but does not impair choice of stimuli with fixed reward association, whereas CDt inactivation impairs only choices with fixed reward association stimuli and not flexible reward (Kim and Hikosaka, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim and Hikosaka, 2013.

claim: Microstimulation of CDh and anterior caudate body neurons spatially biases perceptual decisions and alters decision times with random-dot-motion stimuli.
source: Microstimulation of CDh and anterior caudate body neurons spatially biases perceptual decisions and alters decision times with random-dot-motion stimuli, consistent with a role for CDh neurons in linking cortical visual signals, perceptual choice, and spatial selection (Ding and Gold, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ding and Gold, 2012.

claim: During an attention task requiring monkeys to perform covert perceptual judgments, CDh and body neurons are strongly modulated by the location of a spatial cue, response choice, or both.
source: Finally, during an attention task requiring monkeys to perform covert perceptual judgments, CDh and body neurons are strongly modulated by the location of a spatial cue, response choice, or both (Arcizet and Krauzlis, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arcizet and Krauzlis, 2018.

claim: CDh neuronal activity is driven by a combination of sensory signals, information about behavioral relevance, spatial location, and response choice.
source: These results suggest that CDh neuronal activity is driven by a combination of sensory signals, information about behavioral relevance, spatial location, and response choice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: Activity in the intermediate and deep layers of primate SC contributes directly or indirectly to cue-related modulation of neuronal activity in the caudate nucleus.
source: We hypothesized that activity in the intermediate and deep layers of primate SC contributes directly or indirectly to cue-related modulation of neuronal activity in the caudate nucleus.
evidence: This is the hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: Inactivation of SC on the 'same side' of the brain as recorded CDh neurons changes how those neurons represent stimulus relevance while monkeys are performing covert perceptual judgments.
source: Our results demonstrate that inactivation of SC on the 'same side' of the brain as recorded CDh neurons changes how those neurons represent stimulus relevance while monkeys are performing covert perceptual judgments.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation causes clear shifts in the cue-side preferences of CDh neurons.
source: We find that same-side SC inactivation: (1) causes clear shifts in the cue-side preferences of CDh neurons
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation disrupts the ability of a classifier to uniquely identify distinct task-epochs on the basis of CDh neuronal activity.
source: We find that same-side SC inactivation: (1) causes clear shifts in the cue-side preferences of CDh neurons; (2) disrupts the ability of a classifier to uniquely identify distinct task-epochs on the basis of CDh neuronal activity
evidence: This is a primary finding from the classifier analysis.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation alters the structure of correlations in CDh neuron populations, consistent with reducing the influence of a common input signal.
source: We find that same-side SC inactivation: (1) causes clear shifts in the cue-side preferences of CDh neurons; (2) disrupts the ability of a classifier to uniquely identify distinct task-epochs on the basis of CDh neuronal activity; and (3) alters the structure of correlations in CDh neuron populations, consistent with reducing the influence of a common input signal.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: The results demonstrate a causal link from the SC to the basal ganglia that could alter how sensory signals are used to guide perceptual choices without altering the sensory representations in visual cortex.
source: Our results demonstrate a causal link from the SC to the basal ganglia that could alter how sensory signals are used to guide perceptual choices without altering the sensory representations in visual cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Data were collected from two adult male rhesus macaques (P and R; Macaca Mulatta) weighing 10–16 kg.
source: Data were collected from two adult male rhesus macaques (P and R; Macaca Mulatta) weighing 10–16 kg.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: In each experimental session, data were first collected over several blocks of trials before SC inactivation, muscimol was then injected into SC and the presence of a contralateral saccade deficit was confirmed, and finally data were collected over several additional blocks during the effects of inactivation.
source: In each experimental session, data were first collected over several blocks of trials before SC inactivation, muscimol was then injected into SC and the presence of a contralateral saccade deficit was confirmed, and finally data were collected over several additional blocks during the effects of inactivation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The SC output with access to caudate is almost totally ipsilateral.
source: Because the SC output with access to caudate is almost totally ipsilateral (Grofov, 1979; Harting et al., 1980; Matsumoto et al., 2001; May et al., 2009; Nakano et al., 1990; Partlow et al., 1977), in a majority of sessions we inactivated SC on the same side of the brain as recorded CDh neurons (n = 9 'same-side' inactivations).
evidence: This is supported by multiple anatomical citations.

claim: In a majority of sessions, SC was inactivated on the same side of the brain as recorded CDh neurons (n = 9 'same-side' inactivations).
source: Because the SC output with access to caudate is almost totally ipsilateral (Grofov, 1979; Harting et al., 1980; Matsumoto et al., 2001; May et al., 2009; Nakano et al., 1990; Partlow et al., 1977), in a majority of sessions we inactivated SC on the same side of the brain as recorded CDh neurons (n = 9 'same-side' inactivations).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Data were collected in several 'opposite-side' SC inactivation plus recording sessions (n = 4).
source: We also collected data in several 'opposite-side' SC inactivation plus recording sessions (n = 4).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: SC inactivation reliably produced spatially specific impairments in attention-task performance.
source: SC inactivation reliably produced spatially specific impairments in attention-task performance (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data, with reference to figures.

claim: When the cue was presented inside the inactivation-deficit area of the visual field (cue-contra), hit rate decreased and false-alarm rate increased relative to performance before inactivation.
source: Consistent with previous reports (e.g. Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012), when the cue was presented inside the inactivation-deficit area of the visual field (cue-contra), hit rate decreased (Figure 1D) and false-alarm rate increased (Figure 1E) relative to performance before inactivation.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data, consistent with prior work.

claim: When the cue-ring was outside the deficit area (cue-ipsi), hit rate increased and false-alarm rate showed little change.
source: When the cue-ring was outside the deficit area (cue-ipsi), hit rate increased (Figure 1F) and false-alarm rate showed little change (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral data.

claim: Cue-contra hit rate during SC inactivation was significantly reduced in each session (13/13 sessions; all χ2 >9.5, all p < 0.01).
source: We quantified the effects of inactivation on performance by comparing hit and false-alarm rates before to during SC inactivation with χ2-proportion tests (Fleiss et al., 2013), which confirmed that cue-contra hit rate during SC inactivation was significantly reduced in each session (13/13 sessions; all χ2 >9.5, all p 0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data.

claim: Cue-ipsi hit rate increased significantly in 5/13 sessions (all χ2 >7.1, all p < 0.01).
source: These tests also indicated that cue-ipsi hit rate increased significantly in 5/13 sessions (all χ2 >7.1, all p < 0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral data.

claim: 281 neurons were identified as putative medium spiny neurons (MSNs) across 13 inactivation sessions.
source: This allowed us to make efficient use of each inactivation session, yielding 281 neurons identified as putative medium spiny neurons (MSNs, hereafter referred to as 'CDh neurons'; 171 from monkey P and 110 from monkey R), collected across 13 inactivation sessions (nine same-side: five in monkey P and four in monkey R; four opposite-side: two each in monkeys P and R).
evidence: This describes the neuronal data collected.

claim: A 'continuously isolated' subpopulation of 194/281 CDh neurons were most likely to be identical across before and during phases.
source: First, we used established methods for tracking individual neurons across recording sessions (Eleryan et al., 2014; Fraser and Schwartz, 2012) to identify a 'continuously isolated' subpopulation of 194/281 CDh neurons that were most likely to be identical across before and during phases.
evidence: This describes the method for identifying stable neurons, supported by citations.

claim: Many CDh neurons were robustly modulated by the location of the spatial cue.
source: Many CDh neurons were robustly modulated by the location of the spatial cue, and these preferences changed during SC inactivation in different ways depending on whether we inactivated SC on the same side of the brain as the CDh recording site or the opposite side.
evidence: This is a finding from the neuronal data analysis.

claim: Cue-side preferences of CDh neurons changed during SC inactivation in different ways depending on whether SC was inactivated on the same side of the brain as the CDh recording site or the opposite side.
source: Many CDh neurons were robustly modulated by the location of the spatial cue, and these preferences changed during SC inactivation in different ways depending on whether we inactivated SC on the same side of the brain as the CDh recording site or the opposite side.
evidence: This is a finding from the neuronal data analysis.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation markedly reduced an example neuron's cue-contra preference.
source: Thus same-side SC inactivation markedly reduced the example neuron's cue-contra preference.
evidence: This is a finding from the example neuron analysis, shown in Figure 2.

claim: Opposite-side SC inactivation softly biased cue-side preferences towards cue-contra.
source: In contrast, opposite-side SC inactivation softly biased cue-side preferences towards cue-contra.
evidence: This is a finding from the neuronal data analysis.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation redistributed cue-side preferences in favor of cue-ipsi across the subpopulation of 'continuously isolated' CDh neurons.
source: Across our subpopulation of 'continuously isolated' CDh neurons, same-side SC inactivation redistributed cue-side preferences in favor of cue-ipsi and opposite-side SC inactivation weakly pushed preferences towards cue-contra, independent of task-epoch.
evidence: This is a finding from the population analysis.

claim: Opposite-side SC inactivation weakly pushed cue-side preferences towards cue-contra, independent of task-epoch.
source: Across our subpopulation of 'continuously isolated' CDh neurons, same-side SC inactivation redistributed cue-side preferences in favor of cue-ipsi and opposite-side SC inactivation weakly pushed preferences towards cue-contra, independent of task-epoch.
evidence: This is a finding from the population analysis.

claim: Neither the prevalence nor the strength of cue-side preferences varied significantly with task-epoch.
source: After determining that neither the prevalence nor the strength of cue-side preferences varied significantly with task-epoch (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F; prevalence: logistic regression, smallest p = 0.26; strength: ANOVAs, smallest p = 0.64; see methods for details)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis.

claim: Before same-side SC inactivation, 45% of CDh neurons (63/141) had significant cue-contra preferences and 16% (23/141) had significant cue-ipsi preferences.
source: Before same-side SC inactivation 45% of CDh neurons (63/141) had significant cue-contra preferences and 16% (23/141) had significant cue-ipsi preferences (Figure 3A; all ROC CIs ⊄ 0.5).
evidence: This is a finding from the neuronal data analysis.

claim: During same-side SC inactivation, 16% (23/141) of CDh neurons had significant cue-contra preferences and 34% (48/141) had significant cue-ipsi preferences.
source: During same-side SC inactivation, just 16% (23/141) had significant cue-contra preferences and 34% (48/141) had significant cue-ipsi preferences (Figure 3B; all ROC CIs ⊄ 0.5)
evidence: This is a finding from the neuronal data analysis.

claim: Proportions of both cue-contra and cue-ipsi preferences during same-side SC inactivation were significantly different from those proportions before inactivation.
source: proportions of both cue-contra and cue-ipsi preferences during same-side SC inactivation were significantly different from those proportions before inactivation (χ2 proportions tests; cue-contra preferences: χ2-stat = 27.9424, p < 0.01; cue-ipsi preferences: χ2-stat = 9.3793, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis.

claim: Opposite-side SC inactivation increased the prevalence of significant cue-contra preferences from 28% to 36% (15/53 to 19/53; χ2-stat = 0.6928, p = 0.41) and left cue-ipsi unchanged at 19% (10/53; χ2-stat = 0, p = 1).
source: In contrast, opposite-side SC inactivation increased the prevalence of significant cue-contra preferences from 28% to 36% (15/53 to 19/53; χ2-stat = 0.6928, p = 0.41) and left cue-ipsi unchanged at 19% (10/53; χ2-stat = 0, p = 1; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B; all ROC CIs ⊄ 0.5).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis.

claim: The change in cue-side preferences caused by SC inactivation did not result from a unilateral shift, but rather from a biased redistribution of preferences.
source: The change in cue-side preferences caused by SC inactivation did not result from a unilateral shift, but rather from a biased redistribution of preferences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of preference distributions.

claim: Of the 63 neurons with a significant cue-contra preference before same-side SC inactivation, 22% (14/63) retained cue-contra preference, 22% switched to cue-ipsi, and the remaining 56% (35/63) had no-preference during inactivation.
source: For example, of the 63 neurons with a significant cue-contra preference before same-side SC inactivation (Figure 3C), 22% (14/63) retained cue-contra preference, 22% switched to cue-ipsi, and the remaining 56% (35/63) had no-preference during inactivation.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of preference changes.

claim: The loss of SC activity during inactivation reduced the overall prevalence of cue-contra preferences but did not simply shift the preferences of each neuron.
source: These results indicate that the loss of SC activity during inactivation reduced the overall prevalence of cue-contra preferences but did not simply shift the preferences of each neuron.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of preference distributions.

claim: Analysis of the independent subpopulations of CDh neurons validated findings from the continuously isolated single neurons.
source: Analysis of the independent subpopulations of CDh neurons validated our findings from the continuously isolated single neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the consistency of findings across analysis methods.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation decreased the proportion of CDh neurons with significant cue-contra preferences from 25% to 10% and increased cue-ipsi preferences from 15% to 25%.
source: Same-side SC inactivation decreased the proportion of CDh neurons with significant cue-contra preferences from 25% to 10% and increased cue-ipsi preferences from 15% to 25% (Figure 4A,B,E,F; all ROC CIs ⊄ 0.5; see Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2 for monkey-specific data).
evidence: This is a finding from the independent subpopulation analysis.

claim: Opposite-side SC inactivation increased the proportion of significant cue-contra preferences from 13 to 18% and decreased cue-ipsi from 17 to 13%.
source: Opposite-side SC inactivation increased the proportion of significant cue-contra preferences from 13 to 18% and decreased cue-ipsi from 17 to 13% (Figure 4C,D,G,H; all ROC CIs ⊄ 0.5; all percentages collapsed across task-epochs).
evidence: This is a finding from the independent subpopulation analysis.

claim: Same-side inactivation significantly reduced the proportion of cue-contra preferring CDh units (tStat = −3.2336, p < 0.01) and increased the proportion preferring cue-ipsi (interaction term; tStat = 4.2445, p << 0.01).
source: This analysis confirmed that same-side inactivation significantly reduced the proportion of cue-contra preferring CDh units (tStat = −3.2336, p < 0.01) and increased the proportion preferring cue-ipsi (interaction term; tStat = 4.2445, p << 0.01)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from logistic regression analysis.

claim: Opposite-side inactivation had no significant effect on the proportion of units preferring either cue-contra (tStat = 0.5689, p = 0.57) or cue-ipsi (interaction term; tStat = −1.1691, p = 0.24).
source: whereas opposite-side inactivation had no significant effect on the proportion of units preferring either cue-contra (tStat = 0.5689, p = 0.57) or cue-ipsi (interaction term; tStat = −1.1691, p = 0.24).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from logistic regression analysis.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation caused the skewness of the ROC area distribution to change significantly from positive to negative.
source: Quantitatively, same-side SC inactivation caused the skewness of the ROC area distribution to change, significantly, from positive to negative (before: skewness = 0.12, 95% bootstrapped CI = [−0.05, 0.29]; during: skewness = −0.29, 95% CI = [−0.47,–0.11]; p0.05; bootstrap test)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the distribution analysis.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation caused a small but significant change in the distribution's mean (before: μ = 0.515, 95% bootstrapped CI = [0.509, 0.520]; during: μ = 0.478, 95% CI = [0.474, 0.482]; p < 0.05).
source: and caused a small but significant change in the distribution's mean (before: μ = 0.515, 95% bootstrapped CI = [0.509, 0.520]; during: μ = 0.478, 95% CI = [0.474, 0.482]; p 0.05, bootstrap test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the distribution analysis.

claim: The redistribution of CDh cue-side preferences observed during same-side SC inactivation was independent of microsaccades.
source: Importantly, because the SC is known to play an important role in the generation of microsaccades (Hafed et al., 2009), we confirmed that the redistribution of CDh cue-side preferences observed during same-side SC inactivation was independent of microsaccades (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis, with citation to prior work on SC and microsaccades.

claim: The modulation of CDh neuronal activity by spatial cues depends directly or indirectly on activity from the SC on the same side of the brain.
source: In summary, these findings demonstrate that the modulation of CDh neuronal activity by spatial cues depends directly or indirectly on activity from the SC on the same side of the brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The distribution of correlations during same-side SC inactivation was significantly narrower than before.
source: Fitting showed that the distribution of correlations during same-side SC inactivation (Figure 5C) was significantly narrower than before (Figure 5A; bootstrap test, p << 0.01); the width parameter of the fitted table distribution narrowed from 0.071 (95% bootstrapped CI = [0.07, 0.072]) to 0.057 (95% CI = [0.056 0.058]).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Same-side inactivation caused a reduction in both positively and negatively correlated pairs, and an increase in weakly correlated and uncorrelated pairs.
source: A difference of density histograms (during minus before) illustrates that same-side inactivation caused a reduction in both positively and negatively correlated pairs, and an increase in weakly correlated and uncorrelated pairs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Opposite-side SC inactivation caused no change in the width of correlation distributions.
source: In contrast, opposite-side SC inactivation caused no change in the width of correlation distributions (Figure 5B and D; bootstrap test, p = 0.88; fitted table distribution width parameter before = 0.062, 95% CI = [0.061, 0.063]; during = 0.061, 95% CI = [0.06, 0.062])
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Opposite-side SC inactivation resulted in a significant increase in skewness from 0.76 (95% bootstrapped CI = [0.64, 0.97]) to 1.88 (95% CI = [1.68, 2.09]).
source: but did result in a significant increase in skewness from 0.76 (95% bootstrapped CI = [0.64, 0.97]) to 1.88 (95% CI = [1.68, 2.09]), which can be seen in the small increase of positive values in the during minus before difference of density histograms (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation reduced the influence of one or more common inputs to CDh.
source: From these results, we conclude that same-side SC inactivation reduced the influence of one or more common inputs to CDh.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: Removing the common influence of SC results in both fewer positively and fewer negatively correlated pairs, indicating it must ultimately have excitatory effects on some CDh neurons and inhibitory effects on others.
source: Because removing this common influence results in both fewer positively and fewer negatively correlated pairs, it must ultimately have excitatory effects on some CDh neurons and inhibitory effects on others.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation findings.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation primarily disrupts CDh population encoding of the task-relevant spatial location.
source: From these classifier-based analyses, we conclude that same-side SC inactivation primarily disrupts CDh population encoding of the task-relevant spatial location, and also interferes with non-spatial encoding of task-epochs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the classifier analysis.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation interferes with non-spatial encoding of task-epochs in CDh.
source: From these classifier-based analyses, we conclude that same-side SC inactivation primarily disrupts CDh population encoding of the task-relevant spatial location, and also interferes with non-spatial encoding of task-epochs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the classifier analysis.

claim: Before same-side SC inactivation, correct-classification rates were high for all epochs on both cue-sides, with an aggregate of 70% across sessions and epoch indexes.
source: Before same-side SC inactivation, correct-classification rates were high for all epochs on both cue-sides (Figure 6C), in aggregate 70% across sessions and epoch indexes (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from the classifier analysis.

claim: During same-side SC inactivation, classification performance was poor across epoch indexes, with correct-classification rates falling to about 47%.
source: During same-side SC inactivation, classification performance was poor across epoch indexes (Figure 6D), with correct-classification rates falling to about 47% (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a finding from the classifier analysis.

claim: Cue-contra epoch indexes were slightly more strongly affected than cue-ipsi, with correct-classification rates falling by 26% for cue-contra and 21% for cue-ipsi.
source: Cue-contra epoch indexes were slightly more strongly affected than cue-ipsi, with correct-classification rates falling by 26% for cue-contra and 21% for cue-ipsi (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a finding from the classifier analysis.

claim: Misclassification errors induced by same-side SC inactivation were more frequently cue-side errors (which rose by 16%) than epoch errors (which rose by 9%).
source: Misclassification errors induced by same-side SC inactivation were more frequently cue-side errors, which rose by 16%, than epoch errors, which rose by 9% (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a finding from the classifier analysis.

claim: Correct-classification rates were significantly poorer during same-side SC inactivation compared to before (tStat = −2.3893, p < 0.02).
source: This analysis confirmed that correct-classification rates were significantly poorer during same-side SC inactivation compared to before (tStat = −2.3893, p < 0.02)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from logistic regression on classifier performance.

claim: Cue-side misclassification rates were more pronounced than epoch misclassification rates during same-side SC inactivation (interaction term: tStat = 2.2681, p < 0.03).
source: and that cue-side misclassification rates were more pronounced than epoch misclassification rates (interaction term: tStat = 2.2681, p < 0.03).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from logistic regression on classifier performance.

claim: Opposite-side SC inactivation had essentially no effect on classification performance.
source: Opposite-side SC inactivation had essentially no effect on classification performance.
evidence: This is a finding from the classifier analysis.

claim: Before opposite-side SC inactivation, the aggregate correct-classification rate was 71% and rose to 72% during inactivation.
source: Before opposite-side SC inactivation (Figure 6I), the aggregate correct-classification rate was 71% (Figure 6L) and rose to 72% during inactivation (Figure 6J,M).
evidence: This is a finding from the classifier analysis.

claim: Logistic regression applied to data from opposite-side SC inactivation sessions revealed no significant effect of inactivation (tStat = −0.54726, p = 0.5842).
source: Logistic regression applied to data from these opposite-side SC inactivation sessions revealed no significant effect of inactivation (tStat = −0.54726, p = 0.5842), and no significant interactions (tStat range: −0.05–0.075, all p > 0.91).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from logistic regression on classifier performance.

claim: The pattern of neuronal activity observed during attention-task performance in the anterior portion of the CDh relies on output from the superior colliculus (SC), either directly or indirectly.
source: Our results establish that the pattern of neuronal activity observed during attention-task performance in the anterior portion or the CDh relies on output from the superior colliculus (SC), either directly or indirectly, and provide a possible basis for the reliable, performance-altering effects of SC inactivation during attention tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The results provide a possible basis for the reliable, performance-altering effects of SC inactivation during attention tasks.
source: Our results establish that the pattern of neuronal activity observed during attention-task performance in the anterior portion or the CDh relies on output from the superior colliculus (SC), either directly or indirectly, and provide a possible basis for the reliable, performance-altering effects of SC inactivation during attention tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Inactivation of SC on the 'same side' of the brain as recorded CDh neurons clearly and consistently disrupted attention-related modulation in CDh whereas inactivation of 'opposite-side' SC did not.
source: Inactivation of SC on the 'same side' of the brain as recorded CDh neurons clearly and consistently disrupted attention-related modulation in CDh whereas inactivation of 'opposite-side' SC did not.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: SC inactivation redistributed the cue-side preferences of individual CDh neurons, decreasing the prevalence of cue-contra preferences and increasing cue-ipsi preferences.
source: Specifically, SC inactivation redistributed the cue-side preferences of individual CDh neurons, decreasing the prevalence of cue-contra preferences and increasing cue-ipsi preferences.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental findings.

claim: Inactivation disrupted a non-spatial component of CDh activity, impairing the ability of a classifier to correctly decode task-epoch from populations of CDh neurons.
source: Inactivation also disrupted a non-spatial component of CDh activity, impairing the ability of a classifier to correctly decode task-epoch from populations of CDh neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the classifier findings.

claim: Inactivation of the same-side SC narrowed the distribution of spike-count correlations between pairs of CDh neurons, consistent with the interpretation that the SC normally provides a shared input to CDh neurons that was reduced during inactivation.
source: Inactivation of the same-side SC also narrowed the distribution of spike-count correlations between pairs of CDh neurons, consistent with the interpretation that the SC normally provides a shared input to CDh neurons that was reduced during inactivation.
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation findings with an interpretation.

claim: The results provide causal evidence that a novel interaction between the SC and basal ganglia is part of the control system for covert visual attention.
source: These results provide causal evidence that a novel interaction between the SC and basal ganglia is part of the control system for covert visual attention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The changes observed in CDh neurons might be a nonspecific result of the behavioral deficits that accompany inactivation, perhaps due to changes in overall motivation or arousal.
source: Because SC inactivation causes major deficits in the performance of spatial attention tasks, it seems possible that the changes we observed in CDh neurons might be a nonspecific result of the behavioral deficits that accompany inactivation, perhaps due to changes in overall motivation or arousal.
evidence: This is a potential alternative explanation that is considered and then ruled out.

claim: The results from control experiments in which SC was inactivated on the side opposite to caudate recordings indicate that changes in CDh neurons are unlikely to be nonspecific effects of behavioral deficits.
source: However, the results from our control experiments in which we inactivated the SC on the side opposite to our caudate recordings indicate that this is unlikely.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiments.

claim: Opposite-side SC inactivation reduced cue-ipsi hit rates but did not affect the cue-ipsi preferences of CDh neurons.
source: Opposite-side SC inactivation reduced cue-ipsi hit rates but did not affect the cue-ipsi preferences of CDh neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the control experiments.

claim: If the changes in CDh cue-side preference simply followed the behavior deficits, then the cue-side preferences should have changed after both same- and opposite-side SC inactivation.
source: If the changes in CDh cue-side preference simply followed the behavior deficits, then the cue-side preferences should have changed after both same- and opposite-side SC inactivation.
evidence: This is a logical inference used to rule out an alternative explanation.

claim: Same-side SC inactivation decreased the amount of available cue-side information in CDh populations for both cue-contra and cue-ipsi conditions, whereas opposite-side inactivation left cue-side information intact for both cue-contra and cue-ipsi.
source: Furthermore, our classifier analyses showed that same-side SC inactivation decreased the amount of available cue-side information in CDh populations for both cue-contra and cue-ipsi conditions, whereas opposite-side inactivation left cue-side information intact for both cue-contra and cue-ipsi.
evidence: This is a finding from the classifier analysis.

claim: CDh cue-side preferences changed only after same-side SC inactivation, consistent with the anatomical circuits that connect the SC to CDh, which are strongly ipsilaterally biased.
source: These results show that CDh cue-side preferences changed only after same-side SC inactivation, consistent with the anatomical circuits that connect the SC to CDh, which are strongly ipsilaterally biased and discussed in more detail below.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, consistent with anatomical knowledge.

claim: Previous work has shown that SC inactivation can impair attention-task behavior while attention-related modulation of the attended visual feature in sensory cortex remains intact.
source: Although this dissociation of cue-side effects between behavior and neurons may be surprising, previous work from our lab has shown that SC inactivation can impair attention-task behavior while attention-related modulation of the attended visual feature in sensory cortex remains intact (Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Altered attention-task behavior does not guarantee altered attention-related modulation of neuronal activity.
source: This finding demonstrates that altered attention-task behavior does not guarantee altered attention-related modulation of neuronal activity, consistent with our current results.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from prior work, consistent with current findings.

claim: The SC is an especially useful structure to target because focal SC inactivation causes large and easily reproducible spatially specific deficits in attention-task performance.
source: However, the SC is an especially useful structure to target because focal SC inactivation causes large and easily reproducible spatially specific deficits in attention-task performance.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of targeting SC, based on established knowledge.

claim: Previous work has found that the effects of FEF inactivation on attention-task behavior are smaller and less reliable than the effects of SC inactivations.
source: Indeed, previous work has found that the effects of FEF inactivation on attention-task behavior are smaller and less reliable than the effects of SC inactivations (Bollimunta et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bollimunta et al., 2018.

claim: The demonstration that SC activity influences CDh is a reversal of the typically depicted subcortical hierarchy in which information flows from cortex through the basal ganglia to the SC.
source: Our demonstration that SC activity influences CDh is a reversal of the typically depicted subcortical hierarchy in which information flows from cortex through the basal ganglia to the SC (e.g. Hikosaka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the findings relative to established models.

claim: There is an ascending stream of interaction from SC to CDh in addition to the already well-established circuits by which CDh output influences SC.
source: This adds an ascending stream of interaction from SC to CDh to the already well-established circuits by which CDh output influences SC (Yasuda and Hikosaka, 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the bidirectional nature of SC-CDh interactions, with citation.

claim: According to the classic circuit diagram, caudate output, acting through the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe) and substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), modulates the excitability of SC neurons by removing or adding inhibition, thereby affecting saccade probability.
source: According to the classic circuit diagram, caudate output, acting through the external segment of the globus pallidus (GPe) and substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), modulates the excitability of SC neurons by removing or adding inhibition, thereby affecting saccade probability (Hikosaka et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the classic model, supported by citation.

claim: This mechanism can help primates orient towards visual stimuli associated with large rewards and away from those associated with small rewards.
source: This mechanism can help primates orient towards visual stimuli associated with large rewards and away from those associated with small rewards (Amita and Hikosaka, 2019; Yamamoto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are two prominent routes by which neurons in the intermediate and deep layers of SC might more directly affect CDh neuronal activity: (1) through the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), or (2) through the centromedian-parafascicular complex (CM-Pf) of the thalamus.
source: There are two prominent routes by which neurons in the intermediate and deep layers of SC – which our inactivations targeted – might more directly affect CDh neuronal activity: (1) through the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), or (2) through the centromedian-parafascicular complex (CM-Pf) of the thalamus (Krauzlis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge, supported by citation.

claim: In monkeys with V1 lesions, responses of SNc DA neurons to reward-predicting visual stimuli are virtually eliminated by SC inactivation.
source: In monkeys with V1 lesions, responses of SNc DA neurons to reward-predicting visual stimuli are virtually eliminated by SC inactivation (Takakuwa et al., 2017), demonstrating that primate SC can excite SNc DA neurons.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Takakuwa et al., 2017.

claim: Primate SC can excite SNc DA neurons.
source: In monkeys with V1 lesions, responses of SNc DA neurons to reward-predicting visual stimuli are virtually eliminated by SC inactivation (Takakuwa et al., 2017), demonstrating that primate SC can excite SNc DA neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cited study.

claim: When SNc DA signals to caudate are cut off by unilaterally infusing MPTP into caudate, the result is contralateral visual hemineglect.
source: When SNc DA signals to caudate are cut off by unilaterally infusing MPTP into caudate, the result is contralateral visual hemineglect (Miyashita et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Miyashita et al., 1995.

claim: Monkeys with SNc DA signals to caudate cut off are still able to make contraversive saccades when presented with single targets but fail to do so under free viewing conditions or when presented with a pair of lateralized saccade choice targets.
source: Monkeys in this state are still able to make contraversive saccades when presented with single targets but fail to do so under free viewing conditions or when presented with a pair of lateralized saccade choice targets.
evidence: This is a description of findings from Miyashita et al., 1995.

claim: These results are consistent with the contralateral attention deficits caused by SC inactivation being partly mediated by a circuit through SNc to caudate.
source: These results are consistent with the contralateral attention deficits caused by SC inactivation being partly mediated by a circuit through SNc to caudate.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: Neurons in the intermediate and deep layers of SC send a predominantly ipsilateral projection to the CM-Pf.
source: Neurons in the intermediate and deep layers of SC send a predominantly ipsilateral projection to the CM-Pf (Harting et al., 1980; Partlow et al., 1977)
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CM-Pf sends an exclusively ipsilateral projection to the striatum.
source: which, in turn, sends an exclusively ipsilateral projection to the striatum (Matsumoto et al., 2001; Nakano et al., 1990).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Unilateral muscimol inactivation of CM-Pf in monkeys removed the reaction time (RT) benefit conferred by a spatial cue in an attention task, but only for the contralateral hemifield not the ipsilateral field.
source: Unilateral muscimol inactivation of CM-Pf in monkeys removed the reaction time (RT) benefit conferred by a spatial cue in an attention task, but only for the contralateral hemifield not the ipsilateral field (Minamimoto and Kimura, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Minamimoto and Kimura, 2002.

claim: In humans performing a spatial attention task, fMRI data indicated that the CM-Pf was consistently activated by the 'attentional shifts' required in that task.
source: In humans performing a spatial attention task, fMRI data indicated that the CM-Pf was consistently activated by the 'attentional shifts' required in that task (Hulme et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hulme et al., 2010.

claim: These data are consistent with the SC transmitting signals related to attentional selection of contralateral visual stimuli to caudate through CM-Pf.
source: These data are consistent with the SC transmitting signals related to attentional selection of contralateral visual stimuli to caudate through CM-Pf.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: SC inactivation could also affect CDh neurons by other circuits or through less direct network-level effects.
source: In addition to the relatively direct anatomical routes described above, SC inactivation could also affect CDh neurons by other circuits or through less direct network-level effects.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging alternative mechanisms.

claim: Inactivation of the SC is likely to influence neuronal activity in a number of brain areas.
source: Inactivation of the SC is likely to influence neuronal activity in a number of brain areas, and the long-lasting effects of muscimol increase the likelihood that neuronal networks spanning multiple areas will adapt their activity in response to the SC's silencing by inactivation.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential for network-level effects.

claim: The results establish the causal dependence of CDh neuronal activity on intact SC output, but do not reveal the specific circuits or networks responsible.
source: While our results establish the causal dependence of CDh neuronal activity on intact SC output, they do not reveal the specific circuits or networks responsible.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current findings.

claim: The finding that same-side SC inactivation strongly alters CDh neuron cue-side preferences establishes the importance of recurrent interactions between the SC and basal ganglia during covert visual attention tasks.
source: Irrespective of mechanism, our finding that same-side SC inactivation strongly alters CDh neuron cue-side preferences establishes the importance of recurrent interactions between the SC and basal ganglia during covert visual attention tasks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: This interaction includes modulation of neuronal excitability in SC by basal ganglia output and shaping of spatial selectivity in caudate neurons by SC.
source: This interaction includes modulation of neuronal excitability in SC by basal ganglia output and shaping of spatial selectivity in caudate neurons by SC.
evidence: This is a description of the bidirectional interaction.

claim: An abundance of evidence has accumulated for the SC's causal participation in visual selection – SC activity helps determine which visual information is used to guide perceptual reports.
source: An abundance of evidence has accumulated for the SC's causal participation in visual selection – SC activity helps determine which visual information is used to guide perceptual reports (Cavanaugh and Wurtz, 2004; Herman et al., 2018; Lovejoy and Krauzlis, 2010; Müller et al., 2005; Zénon and Krauzlis, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Attention is impaired when SC is inactivated, or when the nodes allowing SC activity to reach caudate are lesioned.
source: Attention is impaired when SC is inactivated, or when the nodes allowing SC activity to reach caudate are lesioned.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from prior research.

claim: Disruption of the recurrent interactions between SC and basal ganglia are a major reason why SC inactivation causes deficits in covert visual attention.
source: Together with the CDh neuronal correlates of SC inactivation we observed, we consider this strong evidence that disruption of the recurrent interactions between SC and basal ganglia are a major reason why SC inactivation causes deficits in covert visual attention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and prior research.

claim: The classifier results are compatible with striatal circuits representing 'belief states' that summarize moment-by-moment environmental conditions.
source: Our classifier results are compatible with striatal circuits representing 'belief states' that summarize moment-by-moment environmental conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the classifier findings.

claim: Belief states can support the identification of conditions that predict upcoming sensory events.
source: As an example, belief states can support the identification of conditions that predict upcoming sensory events (Starkweather et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Starkweather et al., 2018.

claim: If striatal neurons represent belief state, it should be possible to accurately decode environmental conditions from the activity of those neurons, as the classifier results demonstrated.
source: If striatal neurons represent belief state, it should be possible to accurately decode environmental conditions from the activity of those neurons, as our classifier results demonstrated.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the belief state hypothesis to the classifier findings.

claim: The defining features of the attention-task space (cue-side and task-epoch) amount to the task's 'environmental conditions', which can be decoded from CDh neuronal activity with high accuracy (~70%) before SC inactivation.
source: The defining features of our attention-task space (cue-side and task-epoch) amount to the task's 'environmental conditions', which we found can be decoded from CDh neuronal activity with high accuracy (~70%) before SC inactivation (Figure 5; Arcizet and Krauzlis, 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the classifier analysis, with citation to prior work.

claim: The impaired decoding of task-state observed during same-side SC inactivation implies a disorganized underlying belief state representation.
source: The impaired decoding of task-state observed during same-side SC inactivation then implies a disorganized underlying belief state representation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the classifier findings.

claim: If SC inactivation degrades belief state representation, the behavioral effects of SC inactivation during attention tasks amount to errors in estimating the value of responding or withholding responses for task events.
source: If SC inactivation degrades belief state representation, the behavioral effects of SC inactivation during attention tasks amount to errors in estimating the value of responding or withholding responses for task events.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavioral effects.

claim: Some of the behavioral and neurophysiological correlates of attention can be understood as consequences of mechanisms for learning the value of actions or the value of state-contingent action values (sensory-motor associations).
source: In contrast to standard views of attention, which focus on the quality of sensory representations, this interpretation suggests that some of the behavioral and neurophysiological correlates of attention can be understood as consequences of mechanisms for learning the value of actions or the value of state-contingent action values (sensory-motor associations).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: From this perspective, SC inactivation reduces hit rate by reducing the subjective value of responding to cued changes and increases false-alarm rate by inflating the subjective value of responding to foil changes.
source: From this perspective, SC inactivation reduces hit rate by reducing the subjective value of responding to cued changes and increases false-alarm rate by inflating the subjective value of responding to foil changes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the behavioral effects.

claim: The striking correspondence between subcortical structures necessary for attention and those implicated in learning bolsters the assertion that some correlates of attention arise from learning mechanisms.
source: Our assertion that some correlates of attention arise from learning mechanisms is bolstered by the striking correspondence between subcortical structures necessary for attention and those implicated in learning.
evidence: This is an argument supporting the learning interpretation.

claim: Anatomical routes that have been identified as vital for striatal expression of associations between sensory events and appetitive rewards are precisely those that could allow SC output to influence CDh neurons.
source: Specifically, anatomical routes that have been identified as vital for striatal expression of associations between sensory events and appetitive rewards are precisely those that could allow SC output to influence CDh neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the overlap between attention and learning circuits.

claim: In monkeys that have learned to associate a 'conditioned stimulus' (CS) with either an appetitive or an aversive stimulus, tonically active neurons (TANs) in the striatum exhibit stereotypical 'pauses' in spiking for visual or auditory CS presentation, but not for unpaired stimuli.
source: In monkeys that have learned to associate a 'conditioned stimulus' (CS) with either an appetitive or an aversive stimulus, tonically active neurons (TANs) in the striatum exhibit stereotypical 'pauses' in spiking for visual or auditory CS presentation (Aosaki et al., 1994b), but not for unpaired stimuli (for which no association has been learned).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Aosaki et al., 1994b.

claim: Learning-induced responses of striatal TANs require both intact SNc DA projections to striatum and normal signaling from CM-Pf.
source: These learning-induced responses of striatal TANs require both intact SNc DA projections to striatum (Aosaki et al., 1994a), and normal signaling from CM-Pf (Matsumoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Striatal TANs are thought to be large aspiny cholinergic interneurons which can bidirectionally regulate the influence of cortical input to MSNs pre- and post-synaptically.
source: Striatal TANs are thought to be large aspiny cholinergic interneurons which can bidirectionally regulate the influence of cortical input to MSNs pre- and post-synaptically (Ding et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ding et al., 2010.

claim: Visual stimulus-related signals flowing through SNc and CM-Pf to the striatum have the potential to alter the sensitivity of inputs to striatal MSNs by affecting the activity of striatal TANs.
source: These previous results show that visual stimulus-related signals flowing through SNc and CM-Pf to the striatum have the potential to alter the sensitivity of inputs to striatal MSNs (such as those we recorded from) by affecting the activity of striatal TANs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: The same routes through SNc and CM-Pf that likely allow SC to influence attention-related activity in caudate are also necessary for expression of learning-related activity changes in striatum.
source: The same routes through SNc and CM-Pf that likely allow SC to influence attention-related activity in caudate are also necessary for expression of learning-related activity changes in striatum.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the overlap between attention and learning circuits.

claim: Causal evidence has been provided that attention-related modulation in caudate neurons depends on output from the superior colliculus.
source: We have provided causal evidence that attention-related modulation in caudate neurons depends on output from the superior colliculus.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion.

claim: Intact signals from the SC are necessary for CDh population representation of task-state variables.
source: Intact signals from the SC are also necessary for CDh population representation of task-state variables.
evidence: This is a summary of the classifier findings.

claim: The results offer a novel interpretation of attention-task deficits during SC inactivation as the result of altered processing of stimulus relevance in the basal ganglia.
source: Although the specific circuit or network mechanisms responsible for these effects remains to be identified, our results offer a novel interpretation of attention-task deficits during SC inactivation as the result of altered processing of stimulus relevance in the basal ganglia
evidence: This is a conclusion about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: The results demonstrate the general importance of the basal ganglia for the control of spatial attention.
source: and demonstrate the general importance of the basal ganglia for the control of spatial attention.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader significance of the findings.
